Uomo di 35 anni con talassemia major, tr: 35-year-old man with thalassemia major, regularly transfused. 1.5 T MRI for monitoring of iron overload: multi-echo gradient-echo in cardiac short axis and axial liver, 2-chamber cine bSSFP. Ferritin 4,189 µg/L, AST 26, ALT 39, ALP 291 U/L. Chelation therapy ongoing (type and doses not provided by the collection).
Scorri gli echi delle serie T2* nel cuor: Scroll through the echoes of the T2* series in the heart and liver. Is the iron overload the same in the two organs? What is the conclusion?
Il ferro (emosiderina e ferritina) crea: Iron (hemosiderin and ferritin) creates inhomogeneity of the local magnetic field: protons lose phase coherence faster and the signal of gradient-echo sequences falls the more rapidly the more iron there is. T2* is the time constant of this decay: it is measured with a multi-echo gradient-echo (here 12 echoes), placing an ROI and fitting an exponential curve S(TE) = S0·e^(−TE/T2*); R2* = 1000/T2* (s⁻¹). Heart: full-thickness ROI on the interventricular septum in the midventricular short-axis slice (the septum is far from the cardiac veins and from the lung-heart interface, which cause susceptibility artifacts in the lateral wall). Thresholds at 1.5 T: myocardial T2* > 20 ms normal, 10-20 ms mild-moderate overload, < 10 ms severe (high risk of heart failure and arrhythmias: chelation is intensified). Liver: ROI in the parenchyma of the right lobe avoiding vessels; normal liver T2* at 1.5 T is above about 6.3 ms (R2* < 160 s⁻¹); liver iron (LIC, mg Fe/g dry weight) is estimated from R2* with calibration curves (for example Wood 2005). With very low signals the background noise creates a "floor": a fit on all echoes overestimates T2*; truncation of the late echoes or a model with a constant (offset) is used. Liver and cardiac iron do not go hand in hand: the liver loads and unloads first, the heart later; ferritin does not predict cardiac iron. For this reason both are measured. The viewer does not yet have an automatic T2* tool: you can follow the signal of an ROI on the same spot while scrolling through the echoes (arrow keys or mouse wheel) and compare how fast myocardium, liver, spleen and muscle darken.
Fegato e cuore si caricano di ferro con: Liver and heart load iron on different timescales: measure both; high ferritin does not mean a loaded heart.

Il ferro (emosiderina e ferritina) crea: Iron (hemosiderin and ferritin) creates inhomogeneity of the local magnetic field: protons lose phase coherence faster and the signal of gradient-echo sequences falls the more rapidly the more iron there is. T2* is the time constant of this decay: it is measured with a multi-echo gradient-echo (here 12 echoes), placing an ROI and fitting an exponential curve S(TE) = S0·e^(−TE/T2*); R2* = 1000/T2* (s⁻¹). Thresholds at 1.5 T: myocardial T2* > 20 ms normal, 10-20 ms mild-moderate overload, < 10 ms severe (high risk of heart failure and arrhythmias: chelation is intensified). Liver: ROI in the parenchyma of the right lobe avoiding vessels; liver iron (LIC, mg Fe/g dry weight) is estimated from R2* with biopsy calibration curves (the T2* tool uses Garbowski 2014): LIC < 2 mg/g normal, 2-7 mild, 7-15 moderate, > 15 severe. A normal LIC corresponds to a liver T2* of about 15 ms or more at 1.5 T; some tables use 6.3 ms as the limit, but with this calibration 6.3 ms already equals about 5 mg/g. Liver and cardiac iron do not go hand in hand: the liver loads and unloads first, the heart later; ferritin does not predict cardiac iron. For this reason both are measured. In the viewer, the T2* tool (More measurements → T2*) copies the ROI to all echoes of the slice and shows the curve, T2* and R2* with two models (offset and truncated) and, for the liver, the LIC; by scrolling through the echoes (arrows or wheel) you can also compare by eye how fast myocardium, liver, spleen and muscle darken.
